speakeroldname: Mr. C. W. Carter (for Mr. Harrison):
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I move that the first report of the standing committee on standing orders, presented on Friday, February 5, 1954, be now concurred in. Notice of this motion was given last Friday.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the passing of this motion. Indeed, I am a member of the committee, the report of which is now before the house. There is, however, just one word I rwould like to say and I think I should be permitted to say it.
I have noted with interest that the motion now moved on behalf of the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) is recorded in the Votes and Proceedings of Friday last suggesting that notice of it was given on that occasion. I also notice with interest that although notice was given on Friday the motion does not appear anywhere on today's order paper. In other words, it is apparently being regarded as a procedural motion which it is proper for a private member to move so long as the required 48 hours' notice has been given.
When one couples this with the ruling that Your Honour made in connection with another matter last week, it seems to me that a definite practice is being established. I have no objection, but I do wish to draw attention to it so that on future occasions when other private members find themselves in a similar position and wish to move procedural motions comparable to this one they may be accorded the same privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Since the hon. member has raised the point, perhaps I should remark here that it might be well for us to consider whether motions such as this should not be inscribed on the order paper under the title "Motions", so that they would appear on the order paper and no hon. member would be caught by surprise. This might well be considered by the standing committee on procedure.

The government has not received any representations from the governments of British Columbia or the United States, and it does not see any adequate reason to initiate any such discussions itself. So far as the Yukon is concerned, for which the federal government has complete responsibility, there are not at this time nor do there appear to be in prospect any problems of development that require the establishment of "corridors".
Goods to and from the Yukon, as hon. members are aware, are now transported through the Alaska panhandle. I have been told by businessmen in daily contact with these matters that goods from Vancouver destined for Whitehorse, or vice versa, which are shipped through Skagway in bond, are handled by the customs with no delay or inconvenience at all.
Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed to do so, I should like to make this further statement. Some of the discussion with regard to corridors has stressed the importance of securing an area where industrial sites can be established on or near tidewater. I think there has been a tendency to overlook the significance of the word "near". Many large industrial plants, even when located right at the water's edge, find it necessary to load their raw materials into railroad cars to transport them to stockpiles or to various sections of the plant. If this has to be done anyway, it adds relatively little to the cost to transport the material a few miles from the seaboard. For example, the aluminum industry at Arvida is generally regarded as being located at tidewater, yet in fact the plant is about 20 miles from Port Alfred, where the raw material is unloaded from ocean-going vessels and where finished products are shipped.

The house resumed, from Friday, February 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. 168, to amend the Post Office Act-Mr. Cote- Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Rates on letters.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Since the minister has given as one of the reasons for an increase in the postal rate the introduction of the five-day 40-hour week, the manner in which this change in delivery is to be worked out becomes a question of considerable importance. Several reports have appeared within the last few days, both in the press and over the radio, with reference to staff which is to be eliminated. I am very much concerned about this because I cannot believe that some of the reports which I have heard can be correct. Will the minister tell us just how he intends to proceed under the 40-hour week?
Actually, the letter carriers are working a 48-hour week, and then having a liquidation week every eleven weeks. For the purposes of this system a staff was employed to work in the liquidation weeks. I understand that plans are under way whereby the regular staff will work five days a week, Monday through Friday, and that casual help will be brought in to work on the Saturday.

Post Office Act
Now, this does two things, if it is true. It removes from the post office the liquidation staffs which, in the city of Hamilton, I am given to understand, number eleven employees, men who are experienced letter carriers, and substitutes in their place whatever casual help the Post Office Department may be able to pick up at the offered rate of $1 per hour.
In an effort to secure this casual help I understand the officials of the department have been soliciting the universities and high schools to ascertain if students at those institutions would care to undertake this work at $1 per hour. I understand also that the regular post office employees have been solicited and, regardless of the rate at which they are paid, have been offered this Saturday work at $1 per hour. Quite apart from the fact that they have been offered the work I understand that they have been told, whether or not they volunteer, they shall be called upon if necessary to perform these duties on Saturday.
I believe this house would be interested in knowing whether it is the Postmaster General's intention to utilize the liquidation staff where it is his intention to institute the five-day week, or whether he is considering the rotation of the staff to permit experienced letter carriers to carry the mails on Saturday, or whether the rumour which I have heard-I may say that I heard the announcement over the radio this morning-to the effect that the post office is soliciting casual help from all and sundry, is true. Will the Postmaster General please tell us?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
The principle of the five-day week is to permit the employees to work five days or 40 hours per week. It is applied, as we understand, because we want them to work no more than five days or 40 hours per week. We will not force employees to work more than that. But if amongst those who are already working there are some who want to work in their spare time, we would certainly consider their application.
Now, we are going to employ some other people to work the time necessary to complete the week. It will be understood that, although we want to give the privilege to our employees of working the five-day week, at the same time we want to keep the best service possible. In some places it would disrupt the service for a new man to come in and try to get used to several routes. This would cause delay and difficulty. By adopting the scheme we have in mind, we will be in a better position to give service because the same man will be on the same route every day except Saturday.

For the information of the house as well as the hon. member, I might say that we are recruiting as well some clerical staff, so there will be openings there for spare carriers. A delegation from the letter carriers association has endorsed our scheme. I do not know if I have made myself clear, but since we are applying the 40-hour week we want to give those employees who do not want to work more than 40 hours that privilege. We want also to keep this service as speedy and as efficient as it was before.

speechtext: If I understand the minister correctly, he is now telling us that the casual employees he hopes to recruit will do a better job than by taking the experienced letter carrier and putting him on a different route. Do I understand the minister to have said that?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: I do not want to be misinterpreted by the hon. member. We want to have the same service we are giving every day, but the rotating service suggested by the hon. member would mean that the newcomers would have to learn at least eleven different walks, and they would have to take a new route every day.

On this point, within the last few days there have been serious complaints from Vancouver. Apparently Mr. MacNabb of the minister's department was out on the west coast the week before last, and announced that probably there would be a plan of hiring high school students. I have here a press dispatch of February 1 taken from the Vancouver Sun, which says:
Post office authorities are considering the hiring of casual help, including high school students, to make Saturday deliveries of the mail when the five-day week for most postmen becomes effective on April 1.
This was the report of R. H. MacNabb, manager of postal operations, Ottawa, when he visited Vancouver at the week end.
He said in an interview that regular postmen also will be given the opportunity of making extra money by working on Saturdays if they want to.
Now, that seems a very unusual way to bring the five-day week into operation. Surely private industry does not have to resort to measures of that kind when it brings in a five-day week. The postmen in Vancouver have been protesting very bitterly. Other newspaper dispatches say that the protests will centre around the employment of casual help by the post office at substandard wages, and the reduction of professional post office standards by the employment of unsupervised and inexperienced people to handle public property as valuable and vital as the mails.
Union officials are reported to have recommended that the only permanent solution to providing a five-day week for postmen is for the department to hire extra postmen for every five walks in the city.
Some such plan as that I mentioned last would seem to be the businesslike way to bring in this five-day week. Why is it necessary to go out and hire high school students on a temporary basis in order to meet this situation?

The Minister of Finance explained to the house that the five-day 40-hour week was creating a great problem in the Post Office Department. We have understood that, and I think now everyone understands it. When the Minister of Finance announced the postage increase in his statement to the house on Tuesday, December 8, as recorded in Hansard at page 691 he said:
The government has accordingly decided to recommend the following adjustments in first-class postage rates effective April 1, 1954:
1. A general increase of one cent per ounce over existing rates.
I should like to know how far that policy of the one-cent increase is to be carried. The bill that is now before us amends only one section of the Post Office Act, namely, section 10, which sets the rates of postage on letters posted in Canada for delivery in Canada. In respect of what the bill does we are clear. It raises the present four-cent rate on letters from one area of Canada to another to five cents, and it raises the present drop letter rate from three cents to four cents. In addition, it raises by one cent the rate for additional ounces where a letter is overweight. But the question that comes to my mind has to do with postcards. I have been asked whether the rate on postcards is to be increased.
When one looks at the bill he finds no reference to postcards; but I have been rummaging around in the Post Office Act to try to find where the rate for postcards is set, and I do not find it there at all. It looks to me as though the rate for postcards is probably set under section 6 (d) of the Post Office Act, which gives the Postmaster General the authority to make regulations:
(d) establishing rates of postage on any class of mailable matter for which the rate is not established by this act.
I hope the Postmaster General will correct me if I am wrong. I take it from that, and from looking through the act generally, that since there is no rate for postcards set in the act, the rate is fixed by the Postmaster General under the authority conferred upon him under section 6 (d). I assume it is under that authority that we have the present rate for postcards. I want to know, and I hope the Postmaster General can give us a clear and categorical answer on this, whether there is any intention on the part of the Postmaster General, either with or without the advice of his colleagues in the cabinet, to raise the rates on postcards after this bill has gone through. bill can go through and by statute parliament, over our opposition, might increase the rates on first-class matter, but it would still be possible after the act had received royal assent for the government to decide to increase the rates on postcards or to increase the rates on letters which are unsealed, that rate that people make use of at Christmastime in sending out Christmas cards, for example. I hope the minister will not think that I am unfair when I ask for a categorical statement that it is not the intention of the government to raise any of the other rates except the one that is being raised by the bill that is now before the house.

Yes. I have stated quite candidly that I have no intention of implying false pretences with respect to the Postmaster General. The basis of the statement that our consent to this legislation was obtained without our appreciating what we were being asked to consent to is to be found at page 1107 of Hansard. This bill is based upon a resolution which the Postmaster General introduced for the government on January 14. The resolution said that it was expedient to amend the Post Office Aot to increase the rates of postage on letters posted in Canada from the first day of April, 1954. The resolution referred exclusively and entirely to letters. Nothing was said about postcards there or any other form of mail. In explaining to the house why they were asking for approval of the resolution and of the legislation which would be based on it, the Postmaster General explained that they were anticipating a deficit of $13| million. As reported at page 1102 of Hansard he went on to say this:
Expected net revenues from the increase in postage rates will be approximately $14 million, leaving only $500,000 to take care of possible normal increases in the price of basic materials . . .
And so on. It is true that in those words he said: "Expected net revenues from the increase in postage rates". While I think it was only logical to expect that we would take the words as applying to the increase resulting from this bill-that is this increase -nevertheless I realize that a loophole or an escape-hatch, if you like, was left in the words used here "the increase in postage rates", not this increase.

Post Office Act
$13,500,000 extra to cover the anticipated deficit. He said that "this increase" was expected to cover the anticipated deficit.
It is on that basis, sir, that I made the statement that the government obtained the consent of the house to this legislation by something which falls not very far short of false pretence. I have now shown that these words were conclusive and that my statement is thoroughly justified. Therefore I think the government must agree that it has followed a most reprehensible course in its relationship and dealings with the house so far as this legislation is concerned, and I submit without further ado that the Postmaster General should withdraw the bill and not proceed further with it at this session.

. . . this resolution proposes an amendment to the Post Office Act to increase the rates of postage in the way indicated in the resolution itself, . . .
Later on in that same column, after outlining the deficit which, according to his calculation, would amount to $13,500,000, he said:
Expected net revenues from the increase in postage rates will be approximately $14 million, . . .
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that all of us in the house had the right to assume, when the Postmaster General said he proposed to increase the rates of postage in the way indicated in the resolution itself, and when he said he proposed to raise $14 million by means of that increase, that all that was being talked about was an increase in the rates on letters.

We propose to get those funds by means of this increase, . . .
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if there were any way of securing a poll of Liberal members we would get the opinion from them that all the way along the house was led to assume that what was being talked about was an increase on letters only. It is hardly playing fair with the house for the Postmaster General or the Secretary of State to say now that no reference was made to this on the resolution stage because there was no occasion for it. He went all over the lot and dealt with most of the arguments advanced on this side in considerable detail. a good many times, but seldom have I seen a proceeding which seemed to me to be quite so unfair. The minister says it is routine; it is automatic. It is not even that. I am pleased to hear that. No doubt the Postmaster General will remember that I recommended that procedure just a year ago. I am pleased that he has taken this step, although I did not expect that he would raise the rate on drop letters in order to conform to the rates along the rural mail routes.
There is one anomaly which I want to bring to his attention, and it is this. In those areas adjacent to a large city, many years ago there sprang up a number of small, independent, accounting post offices. I do not refer to the sub-post office of the main post office in the city but rather to separate, independent, accounting post offices on the fringe of the large city area but outside of what has been the ordinary three-cent mail area.
Many of those post offices receive their letters for distribution from the rural mail courier, who having dropped the letter bags there then proceeds on up his route and distributes the letters in the ordinary mail boxes along the route, returning and again picking up the letters at that independent post office in order that they may be taken to the main post office for distribution. As a general practice no letter boxes in which the rural mail courier places the letters are permitted within a limited distance-a quarter of a mile-of the post office.
The situation arises that where there is one of these fringe post offices, for anybody within a radius of a quarter of a mile from that post office to receive a letter there it will have to have five cents put on it, whereas if you go on a mile or two miles further, that letter will be delivered by the same man who brought the letter out to these independent post offices. For four cents he will deliver a letter right at the door of the people living along the road. That situation does not seem quite right.
1 can give you an instance in my own constituency. No doubt the officers in the minister's department will be able to look it up. I refer to the post office at Colquitz. On one side, within a quarter of a mile radius, is the city of Victoria where patrons will receive letters at their doors for four cents. On the other three sides there are rural mail routes, R.R. 3, Victoria, where the people will receive their letters for four cents. But in that small island surrounding

Colquitz post office, everybody will have to pay five cents, both those who send a letter out and those who send one in. Quite obviously that is an anomaly which perhaps has not occurred to the Postmaster General and which I feel should be corrected.
I happen to know that in some of these post offices in the fringe area they issue as many as 100 two-cent postage-due stamps every month because letters have not had adequate postage placed on them.
It is a very serious problem for people living in such areas as I have described. Some of these rural routes are quite extended. In my constituency there are rural routes covering a distance of at least 20 miles. It is going to be a great benefit for people living at the' end of the 20-mile route to receive their mail at the same rate. But I have other independent post offices in the fringe or suburban area who are much closer to the main post office in Victoria. They are within five miles of it.
Let me mention another post office, Royal Oak. People there will have to pay five cents, yet they are surrounded by areas where people will only pay four cents on letters posted in Victoria. I would ask the Postmaster General to consider some way by which people living in the fringe areas may receive the same benefits as those living along rural routes. If a rural mail courier carries mail and drops it at a post office, whether it is a sub-post office of the city or an independent post office in the same area, and then proceeds along his normal rural route it seems to me that the people living in what I have referred to as a five-cent island should be treated in the same way as those who live farther out along rural routes.

Judging by some of the discussion this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, this seems to be a day on which various members of this house are being surprised, shocked and horrified. I have to confess that I was rather horrified at some of the things I heard this afternoon, especially when the Postmaster General blandly admitted that on the one hand they were planning to introduce this five-day 40-hour week, and on the other hand they were going to sabotage it. I have to admit that I was somewhat horrified by that admission. I am referring, of course, to the suggestion that in introducing the 40-hour week, they were going to allow and encourage people to work overtime on the sixth day.

In rising at this stage of the discussion I want to say that in my estimation clause 1 should be opposed by all members of this house until such time as the Postmaster General shows evidence of need for an increase in the rates on first-class mail, and until he has carried into effect his own principle that those who use the mails shall pay.
I am not going to take up the time of the committee in reiterating previous arguments which have shown that millions of dollars have been lost on second-class mail, or because departments of government are not paying their share of the cost of sending their mail, which amounts to about $4,700,000. What I wish to discuss at this time is something I do not believe has been mentioned as yet in any phase of the discussion. My point is that clause 1 involves an increase in the postal rate on first-class mail, the only part of the postal operation that shows a profit; and I say that increase should not be allowed so long as the minister follows the principle he has stated, that those who use the mail should pay for it. He should not allow a condition under which some who use the mail do not pay anything at all.
The phase of the matter I should like to draw to the attention of the committee at the moment is this-and I am certain my information is correct-that under the present Post Office Act, or under the regulations, any weekly newspaper in any town of less than 10,000, throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada, can have its papers distributed by the Post Office Department completely free of charge.
I am certain that the minister, being a serious man, will recognize that this does not seem right. It is not right to ask the house to place an additional burden involving $14 million according to the minister's figures, on one part of the operation, while at the same time there are regulations allowing businesses to make use of the mails without

any charge whatsoever. I think if a study were made of weekly newspapers across Canada we would find that they are in a pretty good financial position, yet we find that first-class mail must subsidize another form of postal delivery that contributes nothing toward the cost of the postal service.
Not only is that the policy of this government; it has been the policy in the past. I know from personal examination of the records that about four years ago, I believe it was, a weekly newspaper in a town with a population of more than 10,000 was charged for its deliveries. However, the postal service gave an undertaking that if when the census was taken it was shown that the town did not have a population of 10,000, this weekly newspaper would receive a refund of all the money it had paid. When the census was taken it was found that the population was less than 10,000, and a refund was made. I have the records to show it.
I am not going to repeat arguments that have been made before. But this is a brand new one, and it is completely contradictory to the so often declared principle of the Postmaster General himself that those who use the mails should pay for them. Yet in every town of under 10,000 population the Postmaster General allows use of the mails for no charge whatsoever.
Until this phase of the matter is more carefully investigated, and until the minister puts his own declared principle in operation, we must oppose clause 1 of the bill which asks for a further increase in the only profitmaking endeavour of the postal service in Canada.

a few words on this increase in the postage rates, with particular reference to the 40-hour week. The minister has based practically his whole argument for the increase in rates on the establishment of the 40-hour week, and he accepts the principle of the 40-hour week. It is hoped that the implementation of the 40-hour week will in no way impair the service; but the policy announced by the minister, and apparently agreed to by some of the critics I have listened to, is that the gap that will be caused by the establishment of the 40-hour week will be filled by casual labour or by students.
In my judgment the filling of the gap on Saturday with casual labour or with students will definitely impair the service. A survey conducted in the United States on the very same question led to the conclusion that it will take a casual employee twelve hours to do the work that is ordinarily done in eight hours by a regular 83276-120i

employee. The object of the 40-hour week is to reduce hours, create more employment and at the same time in no way impair the efficiency of the service.
I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to do what was done in the United States under similar conditions, and what is agreed to by most of the people in the country I have heard express an opinion on this subject. That is, the post office should hire one person for every five walks there are in the postal department. After investigation in the United States this was the method they adopted to overcome the difficulty, and they found that their service was in no way impaired.
I think it is the answer to the difficulty in this country. The policy of putting in people who are not interested in the job, and who do not intend to stay there because they do not anticipate there will eventually be a place for them, will not meet the situation. On the other hand, if you hire one permanent employee for every five walks that you have across the country, a permanent employee who will be trained and will stay there, you will eliminate what I consider to be a waste of casual labour and so improve this public service.

Mr. Chairman, if there is one section of our mail which is not subsidized, it is the first-class mail. The first-class mail is paying its own way. What happens to the rest of the mail I do not know. I have not been able to discover the answer to that question, and no other member of the house has been able to discover it. The fact of the matter is, however, that the first-class mail is paying its own way. A couple of years ago the department decided to curtail the delivery service on residential walks, to one a day in urban centres. This curtailment was put into effect and we waited in vain to find out what the saving was. We never did find out whether or not there was any saving. As a matter of fact, in the first year of that operation it looked very much as though the government had lost money, what with the difficulties that were encountered, the extra equipment that was purchased particularly in the way of the storage bins which, I understand from the minister's remarks earlier, were confused with garbage tins, with the consequent result that mail was posted in garbage tins instead of in postage boxes; the adjustment of residential walks and the dislocation of business; the ultimate protests which came in and the endeavours to correct the situation, and subsequently the reversion in some areas to two daily walks. We never have been able to find out whether the department saved money or lost money. It is my opinion they lost money. It is my opinion that it was a glaring example of mismanagement. After the other things that have happened in the course of this legislation being put through parliament, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that it is a piece of impertinence to offer this to us at this stage. In the resolution preceding the bill we had no indication that anything like this would be included. We had no suggestion at any point in the remarks of the Postmaster General that anything like this was up the government's sleeve.
As a matter of fact, from this side of the house we have had many complaints-from the hon. member for Winnipeg North and other members of this group in particular- against the leniency, latitude and subsidizing which has been accorded by the Post Office Department to the publishers of periodicals. We have felt that if any change was to be made in section 11 of the Post Office Act it should be to reduce the extent to which the post office is subsidizing newspapers and periodicals, and subsidizing advertisers in those newspapers and periodicals.
Instead of some attention being paid by the government to the arguments that have been made on the floor of the house, the minister now stands up seven minutes before we are to quit tonight and tells us that there have been representations, not from members of parliament, not from the people's representatives, but representations behind closed doors to cabinet ministers that something be done to make it still easier for the publishers of newspapers and periodicals.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: It would save us some money.

Surely the minister's statement is one we should have the right to look into. The example the minister gave might be a case where some money would be saved. The Toronto Daily Star could use its own trucks to carry its papers to London, Ontario, or somewhere else, and I suppose the minister's argument is that the amount of handling by the Post Office Department might be reduced. But the result is that the Toronto Daily Star might be able to say to the people of London, Ontario, "We are going to get our paper to you that much quicker". Therefore they will be able to increase their circulation, and there will be more copies of that paper being put through a second post office at a subsidized rate. That is the kind of thing that can happen.
I submit that these newspapers are not making this request out of their desire to save money for the government, but are making it because it is something that will be to their advantage. I submit that it is an impertinence to present this amendment to the House of Commons at this stage of the debate. Did the matter just come to the minister's attention at supper time tonight? If not, why-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: It was not requested by the newspapers at all. It was requested by the periodicals. It is merely a case of facilitating the circulation and transportation of the newspaper or magazine. As far as we are concerned it may be more advantageous to the department, because we will save some money. My friend should be logical. He suggested that we should save money on second-class mail. This is one case where he should see a way to save some money on second-class mail. This is a good occasion for him to indicate that he wants to save money on such mail. As far as we are concerned, we only want to facilitate and expedite newspapers and periodicals and at the same time not lose any money on transportation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
The Postmaster General says that this request comes not from the newspapers but from the periodicals. I think he owes it to the house to tell us what periodicals have made this request. He is still telling us that there will be a saving to the government. I repeat my assertion that I am perfectly satisfied that the newspapers or periodicals have not made this request by reason of their desire to save money for the country, but have made it because it involves an advantage to them.
Post Office Act
The Postmaster General tries to say that because we want to save money upon this class of mail we should accept his suggestion and the suggestion of the periodical publishers that this will do it. The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested one way in which this loss could be reduced. If the Postmaster General wants a further suggestion from me, may I say that I have read the whole of section 11 of the act, which is now before us if this amendment is in order, and there are rates in that section that should be increased. I contend that we are already losing too much in terms of post office revenue because of the way we are subsidizing newspapers and periodicals and in turn subsidizing advertisers in those newspapers and periodicals.
In view of the other things that have happened in the house today, and as no attention has been paid to requests from members on this side of the house with respect to section 11 of the act, I submit it is going a little bit too far at this hour to drag in such an amendment which is presented at the request of certain periodicals.
We are, of course, in a difficult position. My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North has pointed out that we do not even have a copy of the amendment. The leader of the Social Credit group points out that they have not received a copy. The page boy said a moment ago that the Postmaster General had only two copies, and one had to go to Hansard and one to the chairman. Did the Leader of the Opposition get one? Well, he does get favours around here sometimes. But here we are being asked to discuss an amendment when only one or two people in the house have a copy of the amendment before them.
I submit that the very least the Postmaster General should do, the very least the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as house leader should do-I see he is agreeing with me-is to agree to allow this matter to stand over until tomorrow. Perhaps I can move that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954

We appreciate the assistance of the hon. member, but I hope we are still capable of running the government and the house. Nevertheless I quite agree that it would not be fair to expect hon. members to pass on the amendment without having an opportunity to see it. Had we reached this period a little earlier in the evening, and had there been some time available to look at it during the past hour, I might have suggested that we do as we did the other day,

pass it in committee on the understanding that third reading would not be called. But there is not time to do that now.
My hon. friend asked one question. As I understand it, he wanted a list of the periodicals that had made representations. I believe the Postmaster General was on his feet two or three times in an effort to read them to my hon. friend, but the hon. member felt that he had other things to say in the meantime. If that is the case, I suggest that the Postmaster General might read the list for the information of hon. members, and then we could report progress and ask leave to sit again.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we shall call third reading of the amendment to the Senate and House of Commons Act first tomorrow. Then we shall continue with this debate. If we have concluded it by four o'clock, we shall call the amendment to the Salaries Act. If we have not, we shall go on with the resolutions in the names of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Fisheries, and follow the program I laid out on Friday night.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, February 9, 1954
